source_refs.excerpt: registry.addHackable(TamableAnimal.class, HackableTameable::new);
registry.addHackable(Horse.class, HackableHorse::new);

rows.concrete_observation: Native registered TamableAnimal and Horse hacks share AbstractTameableHack.canHack: returns (TamableAnimal && playerUUID!=ownerUUID) OR (Horse && playerUUID!=ownerUUID). It does not call IHackableEntity.super.canHack, does not require untamed status, empty owner or player-is-original-owner; null owner differs and another owner also differs. Thus same-owner is the explicit qualification refusal, not universal refusal of already-tamed animals. Default class+alive predicate is not inherited here; server tickEntityHack still separately checks alive when committing. Common registry picks a matching canHack implementation; entity cache can return a prior object between periodic prunes without per-call rechecking ownership. Final server onHackFinished does not repeat ownership guard: stop navigation, clear target, setHealth20, setOwnerUUID(requesting player), broadcast success7, then setTame(true,true) / Horse.setTamed(true). Existing owner is overwritten on the shown path. Animal cat variant branch is same action context, not an additional control policy. Both client finish bodies call handleEntityEvent7; server also broadcasts native7. Finish packet/HUD carries only shared operation entityID/time information, not old/new owner or confirmation the intended owner change was admitted.
rows.application_to_boss_immune: An ownership-changing control needs qualification at final mutation, with a result separate from predicted/local success particles. A check that refuses one owner identity is not protection for other owners. For Boss immunity design, explicit source/target qualification must precede target clearing and persistent ownership mutation; never infer immunity or accepted control from generic tame hearts. This is a research counterexample, not an instruction to add taming/PVP mechanics.
